d1.title: The Multiverse Hierarchy — Introduction
d1.text: Parallel universes are now all the rage, cropping up in books, movies and even jokes. However, they are as controversial as they are popular, and it is important to ask whether they are within the purview of science, or merely silly speculation. They are also a source of confusion, since many forget to distinguish between different types of parallel universes that have been proposed. In this article, I survey physics theories involving parallel universes, which form a natural four-level hierarchy of multiverses allowing progressively greater diversity. Level I is a generic prediction of cosmological inflation with an infinite ergodic space, which contains Hubble volumes realizing all initial conditions. Level II arises when different regions of space can exhibit different effective laws of physics, corresponding to different local minima in a landscape of possibilities. Level III comes from unitary quantum mechanics, where other branches of the wavefunction add nothing qualitatively new. Level IV involves other mathematical structures giving different fundamental equations of physics. The key question is therefore not whether there is a multiverse, since Level I is the rather uncontroversial cosmological concordance model, but rather how many levels it has. The key point to remember is that parallel universes are not a theory, but a prediction of certain theories. For a theory to be falsifiable, we need not be able to observe and test all its predictions, merely at least one of them. Successful predictions of the theories of cosmological inflation and unitary quantum mechanics have made some scientists take more seriously their other predictions, including various types of parallel universes.

d2.title: Level I: Regions Beyond Our Cosmic Horizon
d2.text: Let us return to your distant twin. If space is infinite and the distribution of matter is sufficiently uniform on large scales, then even the most unlikely events must take place somewhere. In particular, there are infinitely many other inhabited planets, including not just one but infinitely many with people with the same appearance, name and memories as you. Indeed, there are infinitely many other regions the size of our observable universe, where every possible cosmic history is played out. This is the Level I multiverse. Although the implications may seem crazy and counter-intuitive, this spatially infinite cosmological model is in fact the simplest and most popular one on the market today. It is part of the cosmological concordance model, which agrees with all current observational evidence. A spatially infinite universe is a generic prediction of the cosmological theory of inflation. The cosmic microwave background radiation allows sensitive tests of such scenarios. So far, however, the evidence is against alternatives such as a fractal universe, a closed universe and a multiply connected universe. The physics description of the world is traditionally split into two parts: initial conditions and laws of physics specifying how the initial conditions evolve. Observers living in parallel universes at Level I observe the exact same laws of physics as we do, but with different initial conditions. The currently favored theory is that the initial conditions were created by quantum fluctuations during the inflation epoch. This quantum mechanism generates initial conditions that are for all practical purposes random, producing density fluctuations described by what mathematicians call an ergodic random field.

d3.title: Level II: Other Post-Inflation Bubbles
d3.text: If you felt that the Level I multiverse was large and hard to stomach, try imagining an infinite set of distinct ones, each symbolized by a bubble, some perhaps with different dimensionality and different physical constants. This is what is predicted by most currently popular models of inflation, and we will refer to it as the Level II multiverse. These other domains are more than infinitely far away in the sense that you would never get there even if you traveled at the speed of light forever. Inflation is an extension of the big bang theory and ties up many of the loose ends of that theory, such as why the universe is so big, so uniform and so flat. Much of space is stretching and will continue doing so forever, but some regions of space stop stretching and form distinct bubbles, like gas pockets in a loaf of rising bread. Quantum fluctuations during inflation can therefore cause different post-inflation bubbles in the Level II multiverse to end up with different effective laws of physics. The possibility of a string theory landscape, where the above-mentioned potential has perhaps ten to the power of five hundred different minima, may offer a specific realization of the Level II multiverse. Although we cannot interact with other Level II parallel universes, cosmologists can infer their presence indirectly, because their existence can account for unexplained coincidences in our universe. Most if not all of the attributes set by symmetry breaking appear to be fine-tuned. The existence of a Level II multiverse implies that physicists will never be able to determine the values of all physical constants from first principles. Rather, they will merely compute probability distributions for what they should expect to find, taking selection effects into account.

d4.title: Level III: The Many Worlds of Quantum Physics
d4.text: There may be a third type of parallel worlds that are not far away but in a sense right here. If the fundamental equations of physics are what mathematicians call unitary, as they so far appear to be, then the universe keeps branching into parallel universes: whenever a quantum event appears to have a random outcome, all outcomes in fact occur, one in each branch. This is the Level III multiverse. In the early twentieth century the theory of quantum mechanics revolutionized physics by explaining the atomic realm. Despite the obvious successes of the theory, a heated debate rages about what it really means. The theory specifies the state of the universe not in classical terms, but in terms of a mathematical object called a wave function. According to the Schrodinger equation, this state evolves over time in a fashion that mathematicians term unitary, meaning that the wave function rotates in an abstract infinite-dimensional space called Hilbert space. Although quantum mechanics is often described as inherently random and uncertain, the wave function evolves in a deterministic way. There is nothing random or uncertain about it. Over the years many physicists have abandoned the collapse postulate in favor of one developed in 1957 by Princeton graduate student Hugh Everett III. He showed that the collapse postulate is unnecessary. Unadulterated quantum theory does not, in fact, pose any contradictions. It predicts that one classical reality gradually splits into superpositions of many such realities. The Level III multiverse adds nothing new beyond Level I and Level II, just more indistinguishable copies of the same universes. The passionate debate about Everett's theory therefore seems to be ending in a grand anticlimax, with the discovery of less controversial multiverses that are equally large.

d5.title: Level IV: Other Mathematical Structures
d5.text: Suppose you buy the Platonist paradigm and believe that there really is a Theory of Everything at the top of the theory family tree, and that we simply have not found the correct equations yet. Then an embarrassing question remains, as emphasized by John Archibald Wheeler: Why these particular equations, not others? Let us now explore the idea of mathematical democracy, whereby universes governed by other mathematical structures are equally real. This is the Level IV multiverse. Logically, it rests on two separate assumptions. Assumption one: that the physical world is a mathematical structure. Assumption two: mathematical democracy, that all mathematical structures exist out there in the same sense. In a famous essay, Wigner argued that the enormous usefulness of mathematics in the natural sciences is something bordering on the mysterious. This argument can be taken as support for assumption one: the utility of mathematics for describing the physical world is a natural consequence of the fact that the latter is a mathematical structure. The Level IV multiverse, termed the ultimate ensemble theory, since it subsumes all other ensembles, therefore brings closure to the hierarchy of multiverses, and there cannot be a Level V. So should you believe in parallel universes? The most interesting issue is whether there are zero, one, two, three or four levels of multiverses. A common feature of all four multiverse levels is that the simplest and arguably most elegant theory involves parallel universes by default. To deny the existence of those universes, one needs to complicate the theory by adding experimentally unsupported processes and ad hoc postulates.

d6.title: The Successes of Inflation
d6.text: Since the proposal of the inflationary model some twenty-five years ago, inflation has been remarkably successful in explaining many important qualitative and quantitative properties of the universe. In this article I will summarize the key successes, and then discuss a number of issues associated with the eternal nature of inflation. The basic arguments for inflation are as follows. First, the universe is big. The visible part of the universe contains an incredibly large number of particles. The exponential expansion of inflation reduces the problem of explaining this vast number to the problem of explaining sixty or seventy e-foldings of inflation. Inflationary cosmology therefore suggests that, even though the observed universe is incredibly large, it is only an infinitesimal fraction of the entire universe. Second, the Hubble expansion. Inflation actually offers the possibility of explaining how the Hubble expansion began. The repulsive gravity associated with the false vacuum is just what Hubble ordered. Third, homogeneity and isotropy. The degree of uniformity in the universe is startling. The intensity of the cosmic background radiation is the same in all directions, after it is corrected for the motion of the Earth, to the incredible precision of one part in one hundred thousand. In inflationary cosmology, the uniformity is easily explained. The uniformity is created initially on microscopic scales, by normal thermal-equilibrium processes, and then inflation takes over and stretches the regions of uniformity to become large enough to encompass the observed universe.

d7.title: Flatness, Monopoles, and Observational Evidence
d7.text: The flatness problem concerns the value of the ratio of the total mass density to the critical density. By combining data from the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe, the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, and observations of type Ia supernovae, the present value of this ratio is equal to one within a few percent. Although this value is very close to one, the really stringent constraint comes from extrapolating to early times, since this ratio is an unstable equilibrium point of the standard model evolution. During the inflationary period, instead of being driven away from one, the ratio is driven towards one with exponential swiftness. All grand unified theories predict that there should be, in the spectrum of possible particles, extremely massive particles carrying a net magnetic charge. By combining grand unified theories with classical cosmology without inflation, magnetic monopoles would be produced so copiously that they would outweigh everything else in the universe. Inflation is certainly the simplest known mechanism to eliminate monopoles from the visible universe. The process of inflation smooths the universe essentially completely, but density fluctuations are generated as inflation ends by the quantum fluctuations of the inflaton field. Generically these are adiabatic Gaussian fluctuations with a nearly scale-invariant spectrum. The predictions of the simplest inflationary models with large cosmological constant, shown on comparisons with observational data, fit the data beautifully.

d8.title: Eternal Inflation Mechanisms
d8.text: The remainder of this article will discuss eternal inflation, the questions that it can answer, and the questions that it raises. The eternal nature of new inflation was first discovered by Steinhardt, and later that year Vilenkin showed that new inflationary models are generically eternal. Although the false vacuum is a metastable state, the decay of the false vacuum is an exponential process, very much like the decay of any radioactive or unstable substance. However, unlike a normal radioactive substance, the false vacuum exponentially expands at the same time that it decays. In any successful inflationary model the rate of exponential expansion is always much faster than the rate of exponential decay. Therefore, even though the false vacuum is decaying, it never disappears, and in fact the total volume of the false vacuum, once inflation starts, continues to grow exponentially with time, ad infinitum. This process will repeat itself literally forever, producing a kind of a fractal structure to the universe, resulting in an infinite number of pocket universes. I prefer to call them pocket universes, to avoid the suggestion that they are round. The eternal nature of chaotic inflation is also established. As the scalar field classically rolls down the hill, quantum fluctuations will be superimposed on top of the classical motion. There is always some probability that the scalar field will fluctuate up and not down. Thus, once inflation happens, it produces not just one universe, but an infinite number of universes.

d9.title: String Landscape, Probabilities, and the Youngness Paradox
d9.text: Until recently, the idea of eternal inflation was viewed by most physicists as an oddity. The role of eternal inflation in scientific thinking was greatly boosted by the realization that string theory has no preferred vacuum, but instead has perhaps an enormous number of metastable vacuum-like states. Eternal inflation then has potentially a direct impact on fundamental physics, since it can provide a mechanism to populate the landscape of string vacua. The combination of the string landscape with eternal inflation has in turn led to a markedly increased interest in anthropic reasoning. In an eternally inflating universe, anything that can happen will happen, and in fact it will happen an infinite number of times. Thus the question of what is possible becomes trivial, and to extract predictions from the theory we must learn to distinguish the probable from the improbable. However, as soon as one attempts to define probabilities in an eternally inflating spacetime, one discovers ambiguities. The problem is that the sample space is infinite. The youngness paradox is caused by the fact that the volume of false vacuum is growing exponentially with time with an extraordinary time constant. At any given time, almost all of the pocket universes that exist formed very recently, within the last several time constants. The population of pocket universes is therefore an incredibly youth-dominated society. Although inflation is generically eternal into the future, it is not eternal into the past: it can be proven under reasonable assumptions that the inflating region must be incomplete in past directions, so some physics other than inflation is needed to describe the past boundary of the inflating region.

d10.title: Everettian QM — Introduction and Overview
d10.text: The state-of-play in foundations of quantum mechanics in the mid-twentieth century suggested that the quantum measurement problem was solved and the way forward was via some kind of Copenhagen approach. However, that changed with the suggestion of new, radical interpretations, including Everettian Quantum Mechanics. These held the hope of providing a detailed understanding of the process of measurement and the relations between the quantum and the classical. In 1957, Hugh Everett III published his dissertation, supervised by John Wheeler, putting forward the relative-state approach to quantum mechanics. Everett's proposal did not treat measurement as a special process and instead argued that in some way, all possible outcomes occur. This interpretation eliminates the need for a projection postulate or any other changes to the quantum formalism. However, its modern version comes with a commitment to a branching multiverse. Indeed, on this view there really are countless alternative realities, or parallel worlds, some of which mirror our own with only the slightest variations, while others are entirely alien. Everettian Quantum Mechanics is not a fringe view and has received much attention from physicists and philosophers alike. It is by a significant margin the most popular of the realist interpretations of quantum physics among surveyed physicists. Modern Everettian Quantum Mechanics is physically unified but philosophically pluralistic. It offers a clean and mathematically conservative account of quantum theory, but introduces a rich metaphysical landscape involving multiplicity, emergent classicality, and indexical probability.

d11.title: History of Everettian Quantum Mechanics
d11.text: To understand the core of Everettian Quantum Mechanics, it is worth looking at the original work by Everett and others in the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s. In submitting his thesis in the 1950s, Everett identified key problems with the orthodox view of the time. In particular, that it included two distinct but incompatible processes: probabilistic collapse and unitary evolution via the Schrodinger equation. Everett's revolutionary step was to construct a theory based solely on unitary evolution. He proposed treating state functions themselves as fundamental entities, allowing for a universal wavefunction that described the entire universe. Crucially, he omitted all postulates relating to observation and collapse. Measurement is a correlation-inducing interaction between subsystems. When an observer measures a quantum system, the composite observer-system evolves into an entanglement where each term contains a definite observer state correlated with a definite measurement outcome. Everett interpreted this literally, such that each element describes an observer who perceives a distinct result. It is through DeWitt and Graham that Everettian Quantum Mechanics became also known as the Many Worlds Interpretation and received more attention. In some ways, Everettian Quantum Mechanics adopts what might be called a naive realism about quantum mechanics, since it takes a direct correspondence between the mathematical formalism and reality. The wavefunction is not merely a calculational tool or representation of knowledge but a real physical object. Everettian Quantum Mechanics solves the measurement problem by giving up the assumption that measurements have unique outcomes and embracing the multiplicity within quantum theory.

d12.title: Decoherence and the Preferred Basis Problem
d12.text: The physics of Everettian Quantum Mechanics is taken by its advocates just to involve the physics of the bare theory. The answer to questions about the modern formulation requires reference to decoherence theory. Decoherence is the name for the set of physical effects that follow from the unitary evolution of a quantum system where interference between parts of that system is radically suppressed. This matters because interference phenomena are our empirical evidence for the existence of superposition states, and where interference between them is suppressed each part of the superposition evolves independently. There are internal and external processes that lead to the decoupling of variables, and consequently to the loss of local phase information and the effective independence of parts of the wavefunction. Decoherence theory is claimed to provide an emergent preferred basis that grounds the division into worlds with the physics of quantum mechanics alone. The problem of the preferred basis concerns how does the quantum state or wavefunction decompose into worlds or branches, and is that decomposition unique. The claim is that there is an effective basis with respect to which the interference between branches is overwhelmingly suppressed by the processes of decoherence. It is that basis in which the branches of the superposition of the quantum state are effectively non-interacting, dynamically independent, and therefore may represent distinct emergent worlds. This basis is supposed to be close to the position basis, because interactions in physics are local, roughly in position: localised photons arrive from the sun, localised particles travel through space, and this basis is thus dynamically preferred for all but coherent systems.

d13.title: The Probability Problem in EQM
d13.text: The probability problem stands as one of the most significant challenges facing Everettian Quantum Mechanics and has probably received the most attention in the literature. While ordinary quantum mechanics incorporates probability through the collapse postulate and the Born rule, the commitment to pure unitary evolution creates a genuine puzzle about how probabilistic predictions can be understood or justified. The problem stems from two key features: its determinism and non-unique measurement outcomes. Everettian Quantum Mechanics is deterministic because the entire wavefunction of the universe evolves according to the Schrodinger equation. More critically, it denies unique outcomes so when a measurement occurs, the world branches such that all possible results actually occur in different branches of reality. In ordinary probability theory, we assign probabilities to possible outcomes with the understanding that exactly one will actually occur. Everettian Quantum Mechanics fundamentally alters this picture such that all outcomes occur, just in different branches. The decision-theoretic approach, initially developed by Deutsch and refined extensively by Wallace, has dominated discussion of the probability problem and become characteristic of Oxonian Everettian Quantum Mechanics. The core strategy is that rather than trying to define what probability is in a branching universe, it asks how rational agents should act when facing quantum measurements. Using axioms like additivity, substitutability, and the zero-sum rule, he showed that agents must maximize expected utility calculated using squared amplitude weights. Whether explicitly acknowledged or not, symmetry reasoning underlies the decision-theoretic approach, self-locating uncertainty methods, and the more physics-focused derivations.
